item.title: Chinese robots shine at LEAP 2026 in Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
RIYADH, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Straight punches, hooks and roundhouse kicks... Two humanoid robots wearing boxing gloves and protective headgear are staging a combat demonstration in the center of the ring. Around them, a wall of smartphones rises, capturing every jab, every feint, while the crowd gasps and cheers as if watching a title fight. This is LEAP Tech Conference in the Saudi capital Riyadh, and the robot fighting ring at the booth of Chinese company Unitree Robotics has become the event's unexpected heartbeat. "I was just passing by, but they immediately caught my attention," Ali Alshaer, a young Saudi who lingered at the ropes, told Xinhua. "I didn't expect robotics to have advanced this far. Their movements are very smooth, their responses quick, and they can perform such a wide variety of actions." LEAP, the annual global technology gathering organized by the Saudi Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and other institutions, runs from Aug. 31 to Sept. 3 under the theme "Into New Worlds" this year. Various Chinese robot products have emerged as crowd favorites, not for spectacle alone, but for the tangible future they unveil in visitors' eyes. At the AGIBOT booth, a large quadruped robot fitted with a "saddle" drew curious onlookers, many lining up for a chance to ride. The AGIQUAD D1 MaxPro, staff explained, is no amusement park novelty: With heavy payload capacity and all-terrain adaptability, it is built for industrial inspections and emergency rescue. "We hope visitors can personally experience the robot's payload and mobility capabilities," a staff member said. Yulia Bekulova, a Russian visitor, stepped off the robot with wide eyes. "This is the future. This is absolutely crazy. Things I read about in books as a child have now become reality," Bekulova said. She added that China is at the forefront of robotics. "China is really changing the world. In the past, it made daily life around the world more convenient through mass production. Now, China is producing such high-tech products, and the world can benefit," Bekulova said. At the HONOR booth, the Robot Phone, first launched in August as the world's first mass-produced robot phone with a fully motorized 3-axis mechanical gimbal embedded into its design, made its overseas debut. A steady stream of visitors lined up for hands-on experiences. "Some functions that once required professional filming gear are now on a phone. This impressed me a lot," said Amr Aljamal, a visitor from Jordan, after trying the phone. "We are seeing so many highly innovative solutions coming from China." Liao Gang, CEO of HONOR Saudi Arabia, called the device a milestone. "Through LEAP, we hope to further demonstrate the rapid development of China's artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and bring more and better Chinese products to Saudi consumers in the future," he said. Liao noted that AI and robotics are important parts of Saudi Vision 2030, adding that Saudi Arabia's robotics industry and market have enormous potential. "We also showcased another two HONOR Robotics models here, and believe they will enter the Saudi market soon," he said. Deng Feng, president of AGIBOT for the Middle East and Asia-Pacific region, said his company has established a team in the Middle East and is actively pursuing local partnerships. Deng said the Middle East is one of the world's most promising markets for robotics and AI. Chinese companies and Middle Eastern partners can complement each other and jointly advance the embodied intelligence robotics industry. After visiting multiple Chinese booths, Chinese Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Chang Hua told Xinhua that this year's LEAP shows a growing number of Chinese robotics companies bringing new technologies and products to Saudi Arabia, where they have received warmth and keen interest from local partners and the public. "China has always carried out scientific and technological cooperation in a spirit of openness," Chang said. "Many Chinese companies are already discussing robot applications with their Saudi partners. We hope these talks bear fruit soon, and we believe more companies will join this cooperation in the future." Inside the ring, the robots keep punching, bearing Chinese labels, but speaking a universal language of innovation, offering the crowd a vivid glimpse of a future where robots are moving from imagination into reality. ■

item.title: Asia-Pacific Media Forum held in China's Guangdong
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attends the Asia-Pacific Media Forum and delivers a keynote speech in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Sept. 5, 2026. The Asia-Pacific Media Forum opened on Saturday in Shenzhen. (Xinhua/Gao Jie) SHENZHEN, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- The Asia-Pacific Media Forum opened on Saturday in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, with the theme of "Building a Path to Shared Prosperity for the Asia-Pacific Community: Media Consensus and Action." Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attended the forum and delivered a keynote speech. Huang Kunming, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and secretary of the CPC Guangdong Provincial Committee, attended the forum and delivered a speech. Participating guests noted that this year marks 2026 APEC "China Year," during which China will host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting. They expressed their belief that with support from all sides, the summit will yield fruitful outcomes and elevate Asia-Pacific cooperation to new heights. Participating guests emphasized that development and cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region depend on the active participation of media. The media are expected to share stories of openness and integration, provide comprehensive coverage of the region's progress and achievements across various fields, and help foster a favorable public opinion environment for the region's open development. Participating guests noted that the media should actively promote outcomes of the series of APEC activities, interpret policies and measures of various economies to support scientific and technological innovation, and build regional consensus for innovative development. They also called for deepening results-oriented cooperation in joint reporting, technological innovation and personnel training, and leveraging media exchanges to carry forward civilizations, spread culture and convey goodwill, so as to enhance mutual understanding and closer bonds among the peoples of the Asia-Pacific. The forum was co-hosted by the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, Xinhua News Agency and the Guangdong provincial government, and organized by the Shenzhen municipal government. More than 400 representatives from over 40 countries and regions, as well as UN agencies and international organizations, attended the event. At the opening ceremony, 16 founding organizations from China and abroad jointly formed the Organizing Committee of the Asia-Pacific Media Partnership Program. ■ This photo taken on Sept. 5, 2026 shows the opening ceremony of the Asia-Pacific Media Forum in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. item.title: Letter from Gyirong: A flag, a ruin and a promise to bring them home
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
by Xinhua writer Zhou Yulong GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese national flag stood above the ruins of Gyirong Port, rising from a layer of debris-flow deposits about four meters thick. Several bouquets of flowers were placed at the foot of the flagpole. When I arrived at the site, the joint inspection building that once stood there had disappeared. The flag was the only thing that remained visible above the ruins. I stood beside a firefighter during his short break from rescue operations. We looked up at the flag in silence, with tears in our eyes. Months earlier, when I first visited Gyirong in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, I saw a peaceful border town surrounded by snow-capped mountains, deep gorges and green valleys. In Tibetan, "Gyirong" means "a place of comfort." At that time, Gyirong was also a busy border gateway between China and Nepal. Agricultural products, textiles, household goods and new energy vehicles passed through the port toward Nepal, while spices, medicinal herbs and traditional handicrafts entered China. Months later, I returned to a different Gyirong. A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on Aug. 26, claiming 31 lives and leaving 531 others missing as of 6 p.m. Friday. The disaster struck suddenly. Many people had no chance to say goodbye. A relative of one missing person wrote online: "She only sent one message: 'I think there has been an earthquake.' We never heard from her again." After the disaster, rescue teams from across China rushed to Gyirong. But a three-kilometer section of G216 national highway near the border crossing was completely destroyed, temporarily blocking access to the core area of the port. The rescue operation continued along multiple routes. Rescue boats searched the river for missing people. Ground teams trekked for more than 10 hours along rugged mountain paths to reach the affected area. Firefighters rappelled down from a village on the east side, while helicopters transported rescuers, equipment and supplies into the valley. When heavy machinery approached areas where victims were believed to be buried, operators slowed down. Rescuers carrying hand tools then moved forward carefully. Before digging by hand, they poured a cup of liquor onto the ground as a gesture of respect and said softly: "We're here to take you home." The sentence was simple, but it reflected the care shown throughout the search operations. From the debris, rescuers recovered personal belongings left behind by those affected by the disaster, including a Spider-Man T-shirt covered in mud and a damaged stuffed bunny. Each item was carefully cleaned, recorded and preserved. As the search continued, another challenge emerged for those waiting for news. Some people stayed awake through the night. Some felt anxious whenever they heard the sound of rain. Others kept their phones close at all times, afraid of missing a call about a loved one. Every night at 9 p.m. in the past few days, Doje Cering, a doctor from the Xigaze Tibetan Hospital, began his rounds at a temporary shelter in a hotel in Gyirong Town. The shelter housed dozens of people evacuated from Laojiang and Risur villages. Several elderly residents had struggled to sleep for days after the disaster. To help ease their anxiety and improve their sleep, medical workers used Horme therapy, a traditional Tibetan treatment similar to moxibustion. Herbal compresses were warmed with yak butter melted over a small alcohol lamp, then gently applied to specific points on the head, chest and palms. While providing treatment, Doje Cering talked with the evacuees about everyday matters. "We can only rest easy when they can sleep soundly," he said. Support also extended to rescue workers who had spent days working under intense pressure. With support from China's National Health Commission and authorities in other regions, more than 210 psychological professionals arrived in Gyirong in three batches. Some counselors with foreign-language skills provided psychological support for families of foreign nationals reported missing in the disaster. Specialists also assessed the psychological well-being of frontline rescuers, providing group counseling and individual support. A psychological care handbook prepared for frontline workers carried a message: "As you protect the lives of others, remember to take care of yourself, too." Standing among the ruins of Gyirong Port, I saw both the destructive force of nature and the efforts people made in response. The disaster destroyed roads, buildings and familiar landscapes. But during the days of rescue and recovery, every careful search, every preserved belonging and every gesture of care showed the importance placed on every life. ■

item.title: Xinhua Commentary: Chinese modernization forges new opportunities for Asia-Pacific community
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
BEIJING, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- As China hosts the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this year, three words stand out in its agenda: openness, innovation and cooperation. They are also three important ways in which Chinese modernization is creating new opportunities for the Asia-Pacific. This is particularly relevant as the Asia-Pacific Media Forum 2026 brings together media representatives to discuss the region's development and future. While the discussion goes beyond the media community, it highlights a pressing question: how development opportunities can translate into broader prosperity across the region. Openness means more opportunities to connect with China's growth. The Chinese modernization is taking place in an economy deeply integrated with the Asia-Pacific. China accounts for more than a quarter of APEC's combined GDP, while its trade and investment ties with regional economies continue to strengthen. The scale of China-ASEAN economic ties offers a telling example. In 2025, trade between China and ASEAN reached 7.55 trillion yuan, or more than 1 trillion U.S. dollars, up 8 percent year-on-year. ASEAN remained China's largest trading partner. As Chinese consumers demand more diverse goods and services and Chinese industries continue to upgrade, this large and growing market creates space for businesses across the region. Openness therefore does more than keep trade flowing. It allows China's development to generate demand and opportunities beyond its borders. Innovation means more possibilities for new growth. Chinese modernization is also being driven by technological progress and the green and digital transformation of the economy. In 2025, China's expenditure on research and development reached 3.93 trillion yuan, or about 551 billion dollars, up 8.1 percent from the previous year and equivalent to 2.8 percent of GDP. For the Asia-Pacific, the significance of such innovation goes beyond the technologies themselves. A vast market and strong industrial capacity can help turn new technologies into products and applications on a large scale. As green and digital technologies become more widely applied, they can create new demand, new industries and new opportunities for businesses across the region. This is closely aligned with APEC's own innovation agenda, as APEC economies are discussing open innovation, cross-border knowledge flows and cooperation in areas including artificial intelligence, digital transformation and green development. Cooperation means turning opportunities into shared gains. No economy can address today's development challenges alone. For the Asia-Pacific, where economies differ widely in their levels of development, industrial structures and capabilities, cooperation can help turn differences into complementarity and make development more inclusive. Chinese modernization places strong emphasis on coordinated development and common prosperity. In practice, China's manufacturing capacity, technological advances and large market can complement the resources, industries and markets of other Asia-Pacific economies, creating more room for trade, investment and industrial cooperation. This is particularly important for the Asia-Pacific, where APEC's 21 economies differ widely in their levels of development and economic structures. The region's diversity need not be a divide. With cooperation, it can become a source of strength. As APEC economies look ahead, openness can widen access to markets, innovation can open up new sources of growth, and cooperation can turn differences into shared strengths. Together, they can help translate development opportunities into tangible benefits for people across the region. This is how Chinese modernization can make a meaningful contribution to the Asia-Pacific: by opening up more space for shared development and helping turn the vision of an Asia-Pacific community into reality. ■

item.title: Exhibition bridges gap between centuries-old Chinese encyclopedia, public
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
A girl views an image at an exhibition featuring the digital version of the Siku Quanshu, or The Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, in Lanzhou, northwest China's Gansu Province, Aug. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Lang Bingbing) LANZHOU, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- An art gallery in Lanzhou, capital of northwest China's Gansu Province, has turned a colossal ancient encyclopedia into something anyone can enjoy. Instead of displaying dense classical Chinese that only scholars can master, it exhibits 122 images from this seldom-presented 18th-century compendium, such as a sketch of an ancient Indian unicorn, a star map nearly a millennium old, and the private scribbles of a stern, diligent emperor. These images form part of a years-long project to digitize a copy of the Siku Quanshu, which translates as the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, one of the most comprehensive collections of Chinese classical works in Chinese history. Compiled during the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911), the book runs to nearly 800 million characters across thousands of volumes, covering everything from Confucian philosophy to farming techniques. Seven copies were originally produced, but only three and a half survive today, preserved in Beijing, Taipei and Lanzhou, respectively. For decades, this massive treasured book was locked away. To better preserve its copy, Lanzhou built a dedicated library in an underground repository with constant temperature and humidity. In 2021, a project was launched to digitize it. By the end of May 2022, the scanning work of the text was finished, and the project moved into data processing. A team of young editors then spent more than two years checking the data page by page, and along the way, they discovered something unexpected: the playful side of the massive and complex text. "Most people think such a book would be too difficult to read," said Zhang Yang, deputy director of the digital publishing center at Duzhe Publishing & Media, the project's lead. "But as we went page by page, we found plenty of vivid images that could spark modern readers' curiosity." What started as a routine check soon turned into a curatorial mission. The team selected 122 of the most striking images and organized them into twelve sections, covering tea culture, astronomy, architecture, medicine, costume, and even weapon-making. The editors gave the sections funny titles such as "Ancient Gardening Know-How" and "Ancient Stargazing Guide," bridging the gap between centuries-old social life and the modern day. One section is called "World Mystery Box," featuring images from geographical works by Western missionaries during the Qing Dynasty. These images depict the Colosseum in Rome, the Colossus of Rhodes, and exotic and mythical creatures, such as lions and mermaids. "We had long heard of the Siku Quanshu by name, but this is our first time seeing it up close," said Liang Tao, a visitor from Xi'an. "It's both fun and awe-inspiring." That reaction echoes the goal of the exhibition. Song Xuejuan, who heads the digitization project, said the exhibition "transforms 'static preservation' into 'dynamic sharing', and turns an academic treasure into a public experience." For a long time, there was a disconnect between traditional culture and younger generations. In recent years, however, new technologies, fresh perspectives, and innovative storytelling have helped connect ancient heritage with contemporary trends. The Mogao Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site dating back to the 4th century, also in Gansu, are an example. In the 1980s, local researchers began exploring digital documentation. Today, they have completed high-precision digital capture of 323 caves. The images rendered on screen are now even clearer than what the naked eye can see on site, revealing details that once required climbing ladders to inspect. Another example is the immersive interactive digital exhibition of oracle bone inscriptions, held in Tianjin in April. Using artificial intelligence and mixed reality technologies, it allowed visitors to experience the ancient ritual of oracle bone divination. The Lanzhou gallery said it had previously received only a few hundred visitors per day on average. But since this new image exhibition launched, it has seen attendance surge to over 3,000 on peak days. Among the crowds were many children accompanied by parents. For Song's team, they were no longer editors merely checking for data errors, but rather communicators sharing the treasures with the public. "I used to think the Siku Quanshu was unreachable," said Song Jia'ni, a 34-year-old editor on the team. "But once you get into it, you will realize you don't have to begin with big history. One picture, or one detail, is enough to hook you." ■ A combo image depicting an ancient waterwheel and an ancient mill is on display at an exhibition featuring the digital version of the Siku Quanshu, or The Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, in Lanzhou, northwest China's Gansu Province, Aug. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Lang Bingbing) Editor Song Jia'ni reviews a digital copy of the Siku Quanshu, or The Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, in Lanzhou, northwest China's Gansu Province, Sept. 2, 2026. item.title: China moves to create phone-free classrooms, help minors navigate digital age
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
BEIJING, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- For Ye Hui, the past summer break has been a digital tug-of-war. Every time she confiscated the tablet, her 10-year-old son found a way to crack the password. So when the new semester began, she finally felt relief -- not just because he was back in class, but because the law was now on her side. "Teachers will be more persuasive, given that the ban on smart devices is no longer just a school policy," said Ye, who lives in southwest China's Chongqing municipality. The ban Ye spoke of is stipulated in a local law on minor crime prevention, which took effect on Sept. 1. It prohibited Ye's son and his counterparts from bringing phones, tablets and other smart devices into school. Official statistics showed that China has close to 200 million underage internet users, with over 97 percent of minors having online access. Minors' attention being eroded by the algorithm is a problem faced by countries across the world in the digital age, said Wang Peng, a deputy research fellow at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences. Putting a mobile device school ban into law is necessary, as it provides legal support for schools to enforce the ban to keep students from such erosion, Wang said. Chongqing is the latest to elevate a phone ban from a school policy to legislation, as the entire country is working to build a safe and healthy internet environment for children's wholesome growth. A similar legal ban has already been put in place in Guangzhou in Guangdong Province, Zhengzhou in Henan Province and places across Fujian Province. The aim is better prevention of internet addiction among underage students, according to Chongqing municipal legislature, noting the provision cited a 2021 guidance document on the protection of minors' rights and interests in school by the Ministry of Education. In mulling over the local law on minor crime prevention, Chongqing's legislative body found that exposure to bad information as a result of smartphone usage caused some school-age children to develop unhealthy ideas and values, and even commit crimes. Ye was one of the worrying parents struggling to keep their children away from smartphones' bad influence. Her son spent nearly eight hours every day on screen and even paid for virtual skins and props for online games during the past summer vacation. "He could always find a way to unlock the tablet." Strict restrictions on smart device use could help nip internet addiction in the bud, Ye hoped. Xiao Junyi, a student from the 29th Middle School in Chongqing, welcomed the phone ban in school, admitting phones had proven detrimental to students' level of concentration and undermined their learning. "We would secretly take out the phone and surf online when class was on," Xiao said. Teachers believe when the phone ban becomes a law provision, it will be more convincing to students and easier for them to enforce. "It will save a lot of unnecessary lecturing," said Hu Ranrui'an, a deputy head teacher at the Science City Middle School Affiliated to Chongqing Normal University. But in reality, some children, particularly middle school students who have no parent to take them from and to school, do need cell phones for emergency contact. "It's not a one-size-fits-all ban," said Jiang Yongsong, a supervisor from the 29th Middle School. There is a provision in the law that allows parents to file a written application if students need phones in school, he said. Countries around the world have also been introducing bans, with smartphones increasingly seen as a source of classroom distraction and a potential threat to students' well-being. UNESCO's latest Global Education Monitoring Report showed that 114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58 percent of countries worldwide. However, experts cautioned that restriction is not enough to address the problem, calling for joint efforts from society, school and family. After physically isolating minors from the digital world, there will be room for efforts to foster their concentration and capabilities for in-depth and critical thinking, said Wang Peng. Ye Hui has already mapped out the reclaimed hours from the screen -- board games on Mondays, jogging on Wednesdays and weekend hikes to replace the virtual battles. "It's about proving the real world can win the battle for his attention," she said. ■

item.title: Xinhua Communication Effectiveness Evaluation Index System releases report on APEC narratives
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
SHENZHEN, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Xinhua Communication Effectiveness Evaluation Index System on Saturday released Chinese and English versions of a report providing insights into APEC narratives at the Asia-Pacific Media Forum held in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province. Titled Sharing Inspiring Asia-Pacific Stories, Contributing China's Constructive Solutions -- Insights into APEC Narratives Based on the Asia-Pacific Communication Index, the report was compiled based on multilingual data resources and intelligent research and analysis technologies of the Xinhua Communication Effectiveness Evaluation Index System. The report takes the period from 2023 to the first half of 2026 as the research cycle and selects over 200,000 pieces of information samples disseminated by more than 200 mainstream media outlets in the Asia-Pacific region. In the report, a quantitative assessment system based on four dimensions, namely communication heat, communication breadth, communication depth, and communication attitude, is established to assess the communication effect of the APEC concept across the region, identify narrative characteristics and communication patterns among Asia-Pacific media outlets, and objectively present public opinion trends and the evolution of Asia-Pacific cooperation under the new situation. The report notes that the communication model of APEC topics is undergoing profound changes, gradually shifting from the "annual meeting event-based communication" to "regular value-based discussion." The shift responds to the common aspirations of all economies to seek development, effectively consolidating long-term regional cooperation consensus and promoting widespread dissemination of the Asia-Pacific community vision. According to the report, openness, innovation and cooperation have emerged as the main themes of APEC communication. Among them, in-depth interpretations of "openness" account for the largest share; "innovation"-related topics lead in growth rate; and "cooperation" has the broadest reach and the strongest foundation of regional consensus. The three themes reinforce one another, continuously building consensus on regional development and creating a favorable international public opinion environment for building the Asia-Pacific community. Given the complex regional environment, the report stresses that deepening synergies and consolidating communication efforts of media outlets across the region are of great practical significance. China will continue to deepen dialogue and cooperation with Asia-Pacific economies, build bridges for mutual trust and communication, and work with Asia-Pacific media outlets to tell the Asia-Pacific stories of openness and inclusiveness, innovation-driven development, and win-win cooperation, contributing to the sustainable prosperity of the Asia-Pacific region. ■

item.title: Xi urges greater efforts to nurture capable young people for socialist cause
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Congratulating a popular national children's radio program on its 70th anniversary, Chinese President Xi Jinping urged professionals in children's culture to redouble efforts in nurturing a new generation of capable young people for the socialist cause. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the call in a congratulatory letter sent Friday to China Media Group's program named Xiaolaba, or Little Trumpet. He praised the program's 70-year commitment to "telling good stories to children," which have accompanied generations of young listeners as they grew up. Xi called on the program's team and professionals in children's culture to fulfill the mission of fostering virtue through education, keep pace with the times, tap deeply into the rich cultural resources, and devote themselves to creating more excellent and popular works that promote the true, the good and the beautiful among children. He urged greater efforts to nurture a new generation of capable young people with sound moral grounding, intellectual ability, physical vigor, aesthetic sensibility, and labor skills, who will be able to contribute to and carry forward the socialist cause. Launched on Sept. 4, 1956, Xiaolaba is the first radio program in the People's Republic of China dedicated to preschool children. It has since grown into a flagship program spanning radio, television, new media and in-school broadcasting. ■
